articles.title: Allyson defende mutirão para zerar fila de cirurgias eletivas no RN | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao governo do RN participou nesta terça-feira (15) de reunião com candidato a vice Hermano Morais e com ex-prefeito de Natal, Carlos Eduardo Alves.
articles.summary: Candidato ao governo do RN participou nesta terça-feira (15) de reunião com candidato a vice Hermano Morais e com ex-prefeito de Natal, Carlos Eduardo Alves.
articles.body:
Em agenda de campanha em Natal , o candidato ao governo do Rio Grande do Norte Allyson Bezerra, do União Brasil, se reuniu nesta terça-feira (15) com o candidato a vice Hermano Morais, do MDB, e com o coordenador da campanha na capital, o ex-prefeito de Natal Carlos Eduardo Alves. A saúde pública foi o tema central da reunião.

Allyson Bezerra se reúne com Hermano Morais e ex-prefeito de Natal Carlos Eduardo Alves — Foto: Luiz Thé/Inter TV Cabugi

Segundo o candidato, a proposta para o setor prevê um mutirão para atender a demanda reprimida de cirurgias eletivas, estimada em quase 20 mil procedimentos. Também estão previstas mudanças no sistema de regulação de pacientes, fortalecimento dos hospitais regionais e ampliação de leitos de UTI.

Allyson ainda falou que pretende reduzir os deslocamentos de pacientes para a capital através da oferta de exames especializados no interior.

"Os hospitais regionais já existentes nas grandes cidades funcionarão de uma forma que nós vamos organizar a regulação. Hoje nós estamos com um problema onde o cidadão de uma região está tendo que ir para outra região para ser atendido. Vamos fazer uma reorganização de imediato dessa fila de regulação e implementar um grande mutirão para que a gente consiga zerar a fila de cirurgias eletivas", declarou Allyson.

articles.title: Concurso de Ipaba tem 240 vagas e salários de até R$ 5,2 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Inscrições podem ser feitas até 8 de outubro. Há oportunidades para candidatos dos níveis fundamental, médio, técnico e superior.
articles.summary: Inscrições seguem até 8 de outubro para cargos de níveis fundamental, médio, técnico e superior.
articles.body:
Concurso da Prefeitura de Ipaba oferece 240 vagas com salários de até R$ 5,2 mil — Foto: Divulgação

A Prefeitura de Ipaba , no Leste de Minas, abriu concurso público com 240 vagas, além de cadastro de reserva, para cargos de níveis fundamental, médio, técnico e superior. Os salários iniciais variam de R$ 1.621 a R$ 5.275,34 , conforme a função.

As inscrições podem ser feitas até as 16h do dia 8 de outubro , exclusivamente pelo site do Instituto Brasileiro de Gestão e Pesquisa (IBGP), responsável pelo concurso.

As taxas de inscrição são de R$ 60 para cargos de nível fundamental, R$ 80 para médio e técnico e R$ 100 para superior . O pagamento poderá ser feito até 9 de outubro. Veja as vagas:

Agente Administrativo da Procuradoria: 2 vagas

Agente de Controle de Tratamento Fora do Domicílio (TFD): 1

Procurador Jurídico Municipal Auxiliar: 1

As jornadas de trabalho variam de 24 a 40 horas semanais, conforme o cargo.

As inscrições foram abertas em 9 de setembro e seguem até 8 de outubro. O edital prevê oportunidades para o quadro permanente da Prefeitura de Ipaba e formação de cadastro de reserva.

Todos os candidatos farão prova objetiva de múltipla escolha. A aplicação está prevista para 6 de dezembro de 2026 .

Dependendo do cargo, o concurso terá outras etapas. Para Procurador Jurídico Municipal e Procurador Jurídico Municipal Auxiliar, haverá prova discursiva com peça jurídica.

Professor, Professor de Educação Física, Professor de Inglês e Supervisor de Ensino farão prova discursiva de redação. Os cargos de nível superior também terão prova de títulos.

Já os candidatos a Gari Coletor, Gari Varrição, Operador de Motoniveladora, Operador de Pá Carregadeira, Operador de Retroescavadeira, Pedreiro, Pintor, Motorista I e Motorista II passarão por prova prática.

O edital foi alterado nos conteúdos programáticos e no quadro de provas. Para os cargos de nível fundamental completo, a disciplina Raciocínio Lógico foi substituída por Matemática .

Para os cargos de nível superior, foi incluída a disciplina de Conhecimentos Gerais . A retificação também detalhou conteúdos específicos para Procurador Jurídico Municipal e Procurador Jurídico Municipal Auxiliar.

O concurso terá validade de dois anos, contados da homologação do resultado final, e poderá ser prorrogado uma vez pelo mesmo período.

articles.title: Aliado de Maduro se declara culpado por lavagem de dinheiro nos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Alex Saab aceitou entregar US$ 195 milhões e colaborar com investigações federais sobre suposto esquema de corrupção na Venezuela.
articles.summary: Alex Saab, aliado de Nicolás Maduro, se declarou culpado por lavagem de dinheiro nos EUA. Ele entregará US$ 195 milhões e colaborará com investigações.
articles.body:
Alex Saab ao lado de Nicolás Maduro em janeiro de 2024 — Foto: Federico Parra/AFP

O ex-ministro venezuelano da Indústria, Alex Saab , aliado próximo do ex-presidente Nicolás Maduro , se declarou culpado nesta terça-feira (15) por lavagem de dinheiro nos Estados Unidos . Como parte do acordo com a Justiça americana, ele aceitou entregar US$ 195 milhões e colaborar com investigações federais sobre um suposto esquema de corrupção na Venezuela .

Segundo os procuradores, Saab participou de uma rede de subornos para obter contratos públicos no país. As autoridades americanas investigam o empresário colombiano há mais de uma década . Ele foi extraditado para os Estados Unidos em maio pela presidente interina da Venezuela, Delcy Rodríguez .

A acusação de lavagem de dinheiro prevê pena máxima de 20 anos de prisão. Os procuradores, porém, se comprometeram a recomendar uma punição próxima ao mínimo previsto e a pedir novas reduções caso a colaboração de Saab seja considerada útil. Ele também poderá ajudar em investigações envolvendo quatro outros acusados cujos nomes não foram divulgados.

Saab havia sido acusado formalmente em 2019, durante o primeiro governo de Donald Trump . Em 2020, ele foi preso em Cabo Verde durante uma escala para abastecimento de seu avião. Na época, o governo venezuelano afirmou que ele estava em uma missão humanitária a caminho do Irã.

Em 2023, o então presidente dos Estados Unidos, Joe Biden, concedeu um indulto a Saab em troca da libertação de vários americanos presos na Venezuela. A negociação fazia parte de uma tentativa da Casa Branca de pressionar Maduro a realizar eleições presidenciais livres.

A decisão provocou críticas de republicanos e de autoridades federais de segurança. Após o indulto, investigadores americanos abriram novas apurações contra Saab por supostos crimes que não estavam incluídos no acordo de perdão .

Saab era apontado como "laranja" de Maduro

Durante anos, autoridades americanas descreveram Saab como um operador financeiro de Maduro. Agora, os investigadores poderão tentar obter informações dele sobre o ex-presidente venezuelano, que foi capturado em janeiro durante uma operação militar dos Estados Unidos e levado para Nova York, onde aguarda julgamento por acusações relacionadas ao tráfico de drogas.

articles.title: Flash floods threaten parts of Midwest, Southwest
articles.summary: Flash flood threats are in place for areas from Kansas to Arizona.
articles.body:
Elevated flash flood threats were issued for parts of the Midwest and Southwest late Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday, potentially impacting millions from Illinois to Texas to Arizona.

A level 2 of 4 threat is in place for widespread areas from the Texas panhandle to central Indiana, encompassing Kansas City, Missouri, Peoria, Illinois and Wichita, Kansas.

St. Joseph County, Missouri, north of Kansas City, is under a level 3 of 4 flood threat, with storms in the area expected to begin late Tuesday afternoon and possibly continue in the overnight hours.

Some areas, particularly northeastern Kansas and northern Missouri, could receive 4 to 6 inches of rainfall overnight.

Continued rain from Tuesday night through Wednesday morning has caused a level 2 of 4 flood threat Wednesday for areas from St. Joseph County, Missouri, to Chicago.

In the Southwest, a level 2 of 4 flood threat is in place for areas in Arizona, Texas, New Mexico and Utah. Tucson, Arizona, Santa Fe, New Mexico and Cedar City, Utah are among the cities in threatened zones.

The flood threat in the Southwest is forecast to persist through at least Thursday.

Meanwhile, on Monday night, severe thunderstorms and damaging wind gusts between 70 and 83 miles per hour took down power lines and trees in the plains of Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska.

Thunderstorms on Monday also brought heavy rain and strong wind gusts in Tucson, Arizona, prompting water rescues.

articles.summary: After meeting PM Modi, 81-year-old Asgar Ali Vora gets disputed Bhayander land back as BJP MLA Narendra Mehta surrenders possession, permits, and complaint.
articles.body: Bhayander: Days after an 81-year-old Mira Road resident met his schoolmate, PM Narendra Modi, alleging encroachment of his land in Bhayander by a construction firm owned by BJP MLA Narendra Mehta, the politician said on Tuesday that he is giving up possession of the disputed land and surrendering the nod for construction granted to him for the plot.Mehta also said he was withdrawing a complaint he had earlier filed against the elderly man, Asgar Ali Vora.Vora studied with Modi at B N School in Vadnagar, Gujarat. He met the PM on Sept 8 and sought his intervention in the dispute. He said he had purchased around 2,810sqm of land at Navghar in Bhayander East in 1989, but in 2011, the plot was taken over by Swayam Builders and Mehta’s Seven Eleven Constructions. Vora said he had been pursuing the matter with various govt authorities for nearly 15 years. He had said he had received a positive response from the PM during his meeting. TOI had on Sept 13 reported about Vora’s complaint as well as the meeting.Following the meeting, govt authorities took up the matter. A meeting was convened at Mantralaya on Tuesday by Shrikar Pardeshi, principal secretary to the CM. Vora, Mehta, Mira-Bhayander municipal commissioner Radha Binod Sharma and town planner Purushottam Shinde attended it.During the meeting, Mehta submitted a letter to the town planning department stating that he was giving up possession of the disputed land and surrendering the construction permission granted. A man in his 20s has been arrested in the investigation into a suspected murder in Jaffa on Tuesday evening, where a 28-year-old man was shot on Rubinstein Street in the city, Israel Police announced.

Police transferred the suspect to the Tel Aviv District's Central Investigation Unit for further processing.

According to police, a report was received earlier in the evening about a shooting incident at the scene.

The wounded man was evacuated in serious condition to Wolfson Medical Center in Holon , where medical teams were forced to pronounce his death.

Large forces from the Jaffa police station, along with forensic investigators from the Tel Aviv District, arrived at the scene.

Officers launched extensive searches for any suspects involved and are collecting evidence in an effort to determine the circumstances and motive of the shooting .

articles.title: Small-business owner urges Seattle leaders to act now on public drug use and slow emergency response
articles.summary: Store owner Matt Humphrey said he called 911 for open-air drug use near his shop and never saw police, as Seattle business leaders demand a public safety plan.
articles.body: As dozens of Seattle business leaders call on the city to crack down on open-air drug markets, one small-business owner says he has been dealing with the consequences firsthand. "It's not getting better, it's getting worse despite the statistics," Matt Humphrey, owner of Steele Barber and Steele Salons, told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "What I've seen even this past week, I had to call 911 a couple days ago for some open-air drug use right around the corner from one of my shops, and they hijacked a whole shipment of produce from a local restaurant and had it strewn all over, were shooting up and smoking something. I called 911 and never saw the police. We just encounter this really every day or every week, and it's, it's dangerous for our staff, and it's not great for our customers, and I just keep pressing on to, you know, tell everyone we can't move, pick up and root up our businesses and just move them." INSIDE SEATTLE’S OPEN-AIR DRUG CRISIS AS FENTANYL RAVAGES CITY AND ACTIVISTS BAIL OUT ALLEGED CRIMINALS Humphrey says public drug use, harassment and slow emergency responses have become recurring problems near his businesses and home. Humphrey said he was encouraged to see an open letter sent Thursday to Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council. The letter, signed by 38 business leaders in the Seattle area including executives from companies such as Microsoft, Starbucks, Costco, Nordstrom, the Seattle Mariners and Alaska Airlines, requested a 100-day public-safety action plan, more surveillance cameras, increased police staffing and faster response times. It also asked the city to prioritize treatment and shelter while pursuing arrest and prosecution for people who repeatedly refuse help. "I saw several things in the letter, the open letter to the mayor that were published here locally, that I think are all encouraging," Humphrey said. "It's encouraging to see big companies. I'm just a small company, but it's encouraging to see big companies step forward and, and demand some accountability for what we really are working hard to do in the city, which is provide jobs." SEATTLE CLEANED UP FOR THE WORLD CUP BUT ONLY WHILE THE WORLD WAS WATCHING, COMMENTATOR SAYS In a recent statement from Wilson shared by KOMO News following the shooting at the Bite of Seattle festival in July that left three people dead and others injured, Wilson said Seattle Police Department data show shootings and homicides at their lowest in a decade. "I think it's getting worse," Humphrey said. "I don't think it's getting better, and that's the tough part. It's like when people throw around statistics, that's not what I see, it's not what I see driving around. I see the tent encampments moving around, blocks from my business, from my home. You know, I called 911 last week with a guy, 20 feet from my house, that looked like he was dead. And what I get is bounced around between the 911 operator and the EMS people. And they're like, would you, ‘Are you comfortable talking to this guy to see if he's OK?’ And I'm like, ’No, he could have a weapon.’ We don't know what's going on. This is the kind of stuff that we're living with in the city of Seattle." Any change, however, would not be effective, according to Humphrey, without the support of the police. "And employee security for our own employees, and we can't do that if we're not supported by the police," Humphrey said. "So, increased police on the streets, increased response times to when we do call. I think those are all really simple things that we can get in place quicker if the — if the mayor and the city leaders put this into action." SEATTLE SENIORS BEG CITY FOR HELP AS ‘ABSOLUTE ANARCHY’ ERUPTS OUTSIDE LGBTQ HOUSING COMPLEX He said he would want to tell Wilson to view the issue as a concerned parent would. "I would just simply say, 'Gosh, you're a mom, you don't want your kids walking by people with needles laying on the ground or walking into your business," Humphrey said. "If you were getting your hair done in one of my salons and getting harassed by people that are completely out of their minds and high on drugs. I deal with that all the time." "I know you're a parent," he added. "It's — you just can't get caught up in the cog of process and stuck with all the policy and all the nonsense that's going on. We just have to make the change now. It just — I've been saying this for six years — we just have to make a change, or we're just going to lose the city." articles.title: China's porcelain capital is crushing broken ceramics once sent to landfill; the waste is becoming new vases, planters and tableware
articles.summary: China News: A broken plate or chipped cup usually has little value once it can no longer be used. In many places, such pieces are simply thrown away, joining a mu.
articles.body: A broken plate or chipped cup usually has little value once it can no longer be used. In many places, such pieces are simply thrown away, joining a much larger stream of household and industrial waste. Jingdezhen, China's historic porcelain centre, is taking a different approach to some of its discarded ceramics. Broken pieces from the city's porcelain industry are being collected, crushed and processed into material that can be fired again. The recycled substance is now being used in products ranging from vases and planters to tableware and architectural materials. The practice is giving an old material a new role while addressing a growing waste problem.The recycling process behind Jingdezhen's new ceramicsThe approach is relatively straightforward in principle, although turning discarded ceramics into something suitable for another product requires careful processing. Waste porcelain is collected and sorted before being crushed and purified. The resulting material can then be reformulated and fired again.According to Xinhua , that is the process behind XUN, a Jingdezhen brand whose name refers to recycling. Its products include vases, planters and tableware, with some finished pieces deliberately retaining tiny porcelain particles from the recycled material. The result is not intended to look like waste. Once processed and fired, the old fragments are difficult to distinguish from conventional ceramic material.The company has also experimented with sand-mould 3D printing, allowing recycled ceramic material to be used for larger decorative objects. Its products have been displayed at events including the China International Import Expo and the Canton Fair, while sales have reached customers in Europe and the Americas.For a city built around porcelain, the idea has a particular relevance. The discarded material is not coming from an unrelated waste stream. It is a by-product of the industry that has defined Jingdezhen for generations.How discarded ceramics helped shape JingdezhenLong before recycling became an industrial term, Jingdezhen residents had found practical uses for the debris left behind by its kilns.Broken porcelain fragments, old kiln bricks and spent saggers were incorporated into the built environment. They were used in foundations, walls and land reclamation, with some material placed into waterways to help raise the ground. In a city where porcelain production was taking place on a huge scale, throwing every broken piece away was never the only option.Some of that history can still be read in the city itself. The name Xianong, meaning "lower alley", is associated with land that was reclaimed from a river using discarded porcelain. What might sound like an ordinary street name therefore carries a reminder of the material once used beneath it.Porcelain waste also found a place in Jingdezhen's drainage system. Pieces were packed beneath roads to create porous layers through which rainwater could move towards underground channels. That was useful in a city vulnerable to flooding.By 1990, the city's sewer network extended for more than 90,000 metres. More than 6,000 metres consisted of arched channels constructed using discarded kiln bricks. At least one drainage channel built in 1914 is still functioning.The material once regarded simply as something left over from porcelain production became part of the city's infrastructure.Up to 90,000 tonnes of porcelain waste are produced each yearThat historical reuse has not prevented Jingdezhen from developing a modern waste problem.Official figures cited by Xinhua put the city's discarded porcelain output at as much as 90,000 tonnes a year. A significant proportion has traditionally been dumped or buried. Unlike many forms of organic waste, ceramic material does not simply break down and disappear, leaving a long-term disposal issue for an industry producing it in large quantities.Zhang Jingjing, vice president of Jingdezhen Ceramic University, said recycling through crushing and reformulation is currently the most effective way to reduce the environmental impact of the waste.The challenge is therefore not just finding somewhere to put broken plates, tiles or other factory rejects. It is finding ways to return that material to productive use without creating another waste stream in the process.Recycled porcelain is moving beyond household goodsThe new uses are not limited to the shelves of ceramic shops.Yi Design, a Jingdezhen startup, works with discarded ceramics to produce materials for architecture and art. One of its products is a permeable brick containing more than 90% recycled porcelain.The brick has applications in so-called sponge city projects, where urban surfaces are designed to deal with rainwater rather than allowing large volumes of runoff to collect on conventional hard surfaces. Such approaches have become part of efforts to address flooding and urban heat.The product received an iF Design Gold Award in 2022, giving an example of how material that was once treated as industrial waste can become a designed construction product rather than simply a cheaper substitute for new raw materials. Instead of recycling porcelain only because it needs to be disposed of, companies are developing products in which the recycled material is the starting point.A zero-waste plan is changing the wider industryJingdezhen's authorities have begun pushing that approach at city level. In 2024, the city introduced a "zero-waste city" initiative aimed at reducing waste generated during ceramic production and encouraging manufacturers to adopt new technologies. The programme also calls for discarded porcelain to be used in higher-value applications.Tong Xiwei, an official with Jingdezhen's ecology and environment bureau, described ceramic waste as a longstanding obstacle to making the industry greener. The policy is intended to cover more than factories, with businesses, communities and residents also being encouraged to reduce waste and adopt more sustainable practices.The timing gives the effort another layer of significance. China released a circular economy development plan in July covering the 15th Five-Year Plan period from 2026 to 2030. Among its aims are stronger systems for collecting and recycling waste, alongside technological improvements and industrial innovation.For Jingdezhen, some of those ideas are being applied to a material the city has been dealing with for hundreds of years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Algeria faces calls to drop death penalty plans after wildfires
articles.summary: Rights group warns Algeria could exploit proposed death penalty laws to suppress domestic political opposition.
articles.body:
Amnesty International has urged Algeria to abandon plans to expand the death penalty and resume executions, following presidential moves to make wildfire arson a capital crime.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the human rights organisation called for an immediate halt to President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s directives. Algeria has not carried out an execution in more than 30 years.

The push to broaden capital punishment sentencing gained momentum following devastating wildfires that killed at least 12 people and injured 54 others last month.

The flames wiped out entire villages across the Kabylie region and other parts of northeastern Algeria, the statement said.

In the aftermath of the fires, Tebboune instructed Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa to amend the law to include arson as well as “child abductors and abusers”.

Anyone sentenced to death could exercise their right to appeal before being executed, Tebboune said.

Amnesty accused Algerian authorities of using the proposed expanded death penalty to target political opposition groups.

The rights group said authorities arrested 20 people pending investigations for arson and subversion – a potentially terrorism-related charge – between July 26 and September 10.

During the 2021 wildfires that left 90 dead, the government prosecuted scores of people on terrorism-related charges, blaming the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie (MAK), an opposition group that the government classifies as a terrorist organisation.

Amnesty urged the government to address the root cause of the climate catastrophes instead of pursuing “arsonists”.

“Accountability for the devastating loss of life caused by wildfires cannot be reduced to pursuing alleged perpetrators of arson,” the human rights group stated.

articles.title: Judge requests federal probe into Philly DA Larry Krasner
articles.summary: A federal judge said Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner may have committed crimes in his handling of a post-conviction case.
articles.body: A federal judge asked federal prosecutors Tuesday to investigate Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, saying he may have obstructed justice and potentially committed other crimes in his handling of a post-conviction case. The memorandum by U.S. District Judge Paul S. Diamond Jr. represents an extraordinary turn of events in the controversy around Krasner’s Conviction Integrity Unit. It was issued as part of a case involving a man seeking to overturn his second-degree murder conviction. Krasner’s office has backed the effort to exonerate the man, Dennis Johnson. But prosecutors assigned to the case have said that it was poorly handled and that Krasner ordered them to “protect the office” after the court began to examine their actions. Diamond ruled that Krasner and his deputy, Matthew Stiegler, could no longer participate in the case. He said there is evidence that they may have sought to obstruct justice, as well as worked to persuade four prosecutors in their office to “urge the court to accept a false narrative,” which would “amount to criminal conspiracy.” “I have thus reluctantly concluded that Philadelphia’s highest law enforcement official and one of his top assistants may have violated the law,” Diamond said in the memo. “In these circumstances, with the issuance of this Memorandum, I refer the DAO, Mr. Krasner, and Stiegler to this District’s United States Attorney’s Office for investigation and other appropriate action.” Krasner pushed back against the judge’s memo. “I respectfully and vigorously disagree with the court’s findings of fact and conclusions of law,” he said in a statement. “I look forward to appealing to the higher court as soon as the law allows. This remains a pending matter, which limits for now my and my office’s ability to respond in the media.” A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania declined to comment. Krasner, a former civil rights attorney known for suing the police, took over the district attorney’s office in 2018. Since he won re-election for the second time last year, his office has faced growing scrutiny over its handling of post-conviction cases. The Pennsylvania attorney general, as well as state and federal judges, has criticized Krasner’s office for pushing to overturn murder convictions without proper reviews. Over the summer, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ordered the state attorney general to review any case in which Krasner’s office was seeking to overturn a conviction. Krasner has defended his office’s handling of the cases.

articles.body: The US military on Tuesday (local time) said it opened fire and destroyed two small Iranian boats this week trying to "steal" a drone ship in the waters off Iran.“Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after CENTCOM forcefully responded," Associated Press quoted CENTCOM spokesperson Captain Tim Hawkins as saying.CENTCOM oversees US military operations in the Middle East and has conducted operations during the ongoing war with Iran.Hawkins described the drone involved as a “Saildrone”, a small craft roughly 25 feet (8 metres) long that can operate autonomously. He added that all of the command's surface drones “remain fully accounted for.”CENTCOM has used Saildrones in the region for several years to monitor maritime traffic. The US military has maintained that the technology used on the vessels is commercially available and does not contain sensitive technology.The development comes after Iranian state media reported Monday that two fishing boats came under attack in Hormozgan province on Iran's southern coast, with several fishermen reported missing.The latest drone incident, first reported by Axios, comes a week after the Iranian navy claimed it had captured a US military underwater drone at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.Hawkins had explained at the time that an Anduril Dive-LD drone malfunctioned while surveying the waters in the region, leaving the US military without possession of the vessel. articles.title: The murder of this female exchange student has shocked Mexico and Spain. Here’s what we know
articles.summary: Authorities are investigating the murder of a Spanish exchange student in Mexico as a possible feminicide, in a case that has shocked both countries.
articles.body: Authorities are investigating the murder of a Spanish exchange student in Mexico as a possible feminicide, in a case that has shocked the academic community in both countries. Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera was reportedly killed during an armed robbery on Saturday in Cuautla, a city in the Mexican state of Morelos near Mexico City, according to authorities. The Morelos prosecutor’s office said it is working with federal agencies on the case and is investigating it as a possible feminicide — in which a woman is murdered due to gender-related reasons — though it has not ruled out other motives. The 21-year-old was studying early childhood education at Spain’s University of Granada (UGR) and had traveled to Mexico just a month ago on an academic exchange program at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM). “Claudia had embarked on this academic journey with the enthusiasm of a young woman building her future. That an experience so closely tied to her education and personal projects has ended in this way causes deep sorrow throughout the Santa Brígida community,” the city council of her hometown in Gran Canaria said in a statement. The university has demanded that the state prosecutor’s office conduct “an immediate, thorough investigation with a strict gender perspective to guarantee justice and prevent impunity.” Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares has also demanded a thorough investigation. “We want to get to the bottom of this,” he told reporters Monday, noting that Spanish authorities are in contact with the young woman’s family. Morelos Governor Margarita González Saravia said state authorities are working to find the person responsible. What happened? The killing happened Saturday night near a cultural center that was hosting a medicinal plant festival. The young woman was killed as a result of an alleged robbery with a knife, according to the venue, which said that staff “immediately notified the authorities” after the incident. She was staying at the center overnight for the festival, the state prosecutor said. “Claudia came to this meeting with the desire to learn, live together and be part of a community gathered around knowledge, medicinal plants, health and collective care,” said the Tlahuilli Institute, which organized the event. The killing happened in a state facing high levels of violence against women. Morelos recorded 21 feminicide victims between January and July 2026, and at that time had one of the highest rates in the country, with 21 victims per 100,000 women, second only to Sinaloa, according to the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System. What is ‘feminicide’? While “femicide” — defined by the WHO as the gender-based killing of women — and “feminicide” are often used interchangeably in English, Paulina García-Del Moral, an associate professor at Canada’s University of Guelph, said there were subtle differences between the two terms in the Mexican context, with “feminicide” focusing more on the broader, structural conditions that led to the crime. Such a case activates protocols that outline how prosecutors, police and forensic experts should carry out their investigations, the professor said. “(The protocols) really emphasize both the use of a gender perspective – which means that they need to be cognizant of the ways in which gender shapes violence, how gender inequality might have affected the life of the woman that was murdered and her relationship to the alleged perpetrator, the context of violence in Mexico and her community specifically – and also the principle of due diligence under international law,” she said. Outrage in both countries Tacoronte’s killing triggered student protests against gender-based violence in Morelos on Tuesday. In Cuernavaca, Mexico, her classmates lit candles and left flowers at a memorial set up on Monday at UAEM’s Institute of Educational Sciences, where the young woman was doing her exchange program. Pamela Martínez, a classmate at the Institute of Educational Sciences, said the community is going through a difficult time. “It is a time for solidarity and respect. We send our deepest respect to her family, her friends and her classmates,” Martínez told Reuters. Frida, Tacoronte’s aerial dance teacher, remembered the young woman’s personality and the way she interacted with others: “I had the honor of teaching her aerial dance, and it was wonderful because everything she did was impeccable. She always had the best attitude, the best energy. She was very smiley and willing to do anything.” In Spain, the University of Granada expressed its “strongest revulsion and absolute condemnation” for the murder of its student and conveyed condolences and solidarity with her family, friends and colleagues. The institution also held a minute of silence on Monday in memory of Tacoronte and reiterated its call to eradicate all forms of violence against women. The victim’s sister, Lara Tacoronte, expressed outrage in an Instagram video, saying: “I don’t understand people or the society we live in. This happens every day, especially to women, and it’s not fair. It is the most violent and cruelest way to die.” What happens next? Morelos Attorney General Fernando Blumenkron Escobar met with officials of the Spanish Consulate in Mexico on Monday “to guarantee justice” for Tacoronte and her friends and family. The governor of Morelos also met with the Spanish consul, Marcos Rodríguez Cantero, to offer more information about the case. “We are receiving admirable and much-appreciated cooperation from the state authorities, and we hope that things will be resolved in the coming moments,” said Rodríguez Cantero. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said her Foreign Ministry is in touch with the Spanish Consulate and that the security cabinet is collaborating with the Morelos Attorney General’s Office in the investigation. CNN has contacted the Morelos Attorney General’s Office for more information.

articles.title: Turkey arrests dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists
articles.summary: The arrests are an escalation in the Turkish government's campaign targeting LGBTQ+ community and activists.
articles.body:
Turkish police have arrested dozens of people as part of the government's recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and venues.

The protesters were detained as they gathered on Tuesday outside Istanbul's main courthouse.

They were calling for the release of another group of LGBTQ+ activists, who were arrested over the weekend in a series of raids on gay bars and at the homes of activists.

The Turkish government has detained members of the LGBTQ+ community and activists as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe", which the government says has been designed to protect family values.

At Tuesday's protest, people chanted "Long live the struggle for freedom!" and called for the detained activists to be released, news agency AFP reported. Police made several arrests after some demonstrators unfurled a banner reading "Being LGBTQ is not a crime".

"What we are seeing now is deeply disturbing," one protestor told AFP.

Rights groups have described a widening campaign against the LGBTQ+ community. Over the past week the authorities raided association offices, blocked websites and made arrests across multiple provinces.

The government has also blocked or restricted access to the social media accounts and websites of dozens of LGBT, media and rights organisations, according to a post from the NGO Human Rights Watch.

Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has described LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.

The Commissioner for Human Rights at the Council of Europe, Michael O'Flaherty, has raised concerns about the arrests.

"I am concerned by reports of a series arrests, raids and the blocking of websites and social media accounts targeting LGBTI civil society and human rights defenders across Turkey," he said.

O'Flaherty's statement said that Turkey's Minister of Justice had said the operation was being conducted against 162 individuals, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces under the coordination of several Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices.

articles.title: Republican congressman calls to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: GOP Representative Thomas Massie has emerged as outspoken critic of war on Iran and overseas military interventions.
articles.body:
United States Republican Representative Thomas Massie , an outspoken critic of the Trump administration’s war on Iran, has sought to force a long-shot vote in the US Congress on the impeachment of Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth.

Massie read articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday, accusing the Pentagon chief of waging war without congressional approval, carrying out extrajudicial killings , and paying little mind to civilian casualties in military operations.

“Secretary Hegseth abused the powers entrusted to him as secretary of defence by subordinating the constitutional limits on the use of military force and the laws governing the conduct of hostilities to his own policy objectives,” Massie said, adding that Hegseth has shown a “profound disregard” for the impact of US military operations on civilians.

The Pentagon chief has faced criticism for the US-Israel war on Iran and his record of disparaging remarks about protections meant to minimise civilian casualties and ensure adherence to the law by US forces, which he has dismissed as “stupid” and “politically correct” rules of engagement that hinder the military.

The resolution for Hegseth’s impeachment could receive a vote in the coming days, but faces long odds of success in the Republican-majority US House of Representatives.

The Pentagon has said that it supports Hegseth.

“The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson told the news service Reuters in an emailed statement.

While polls show that most Republicans support the otherwise unpopular war on Iran, a handful of figures on the political right, including Massie and media personality Tucker Carlson, have become increasingly critical of the Trump administration’s interventionist foreign policy .

President Donald Trump, who pledged to wind down US involvement in conflicts around the world during his 2024 presidential campaign, has previously slammed Massie over his opposition to the war on Iran and efforts to force the government to release the Epstein Files.

Massie lost his primary election in May to a Trump-backed challenger and a barrage of spending by pro-Israel groups .

articles.title: NI woman wants law change to prevent child access for sex offenders
articles.summary: The woman, who is "sick" at the thought of her sex offender ex having access to their child, is calling for laws to change.
articles.body:
A woman who is fighting to stop her sex offender ex-husband having contact with their child has said the thought of it makes her "feel sick".

Lucy - not her real name - described how her "world was blown apart" when her then husband was convicted of possessing indecent images of children, including videos of children being sexually abused.

She told BBC News NI she was further "horrified" to discover he was taking her to family court for supervised access to their child.

She is now calling for a change in Northern Ireland's laws to strip people convicted of child-related sex offences of their parental responsibility.

Commissioner for victims of crime, Geraldine Hanna, said courts had discretion in individual cases but she believed they should be given "all the powers they need" to address concerns on this issue.

"When I think of my husband, who I believed him to be, compared to this person, this person's a complete stranger to me," Lucy told the BBC.

"It makes me feel sick to think that he would be even near my child. So I really do not want to put my child in a room with a stranger, supervised or not.

"As a mother all I want to do is protect my child and I'm not doing that if I'm letting [them] in a room with a stranger."

Lucy said she recognised her call for the law to change was a "huge" demand, but that it was aimed at protecting children and families.

Earlier this year, Finance Minister John O'Dowd committed to changing family law to automatically remove the parental responsibility of anyone convicted of murdering someone with whom they shared a child.

Lucy said she believed that should be extended to anyone on the sex offenders register – which includes her ex-husband.

She said it was a move she thought could also help deter people from offending.

A spokesperson for the Department of Finance confirmed O'Dowd was committed to developing legislation that would provide "stronger protections for children and families".

In England and Wales, Jade's Law automatically suspends parental responsibility for a parent convicted of murdering or committing voluntary manslaughter against a partner or ex-partner with whom they share children

It is named after Jade Ward, who was 27 when she was murdered by ex-partner Russell Marsh in 2021.

However, Jade's Law does not apply to Northern Ireland.

The spokesperson for the Department of Finance said a consultation would be launched this autumn, which would set out proposals for reform in cases involving homicide and "on whether comparable protections should be extended to other forms of serious offending".

Safeguarding expert Marcella Leonard told the BBC that when it comes to people convicted of child-related sex offences, their "right to family life" should be explored by the courts.

This should also be the case, she said, in regards to the child's right to have a relationship with that parent.

However, she said that process should be "bespoke" and based on strict criteria.

"The person must have undergone specialist risk assessment that looks at why they did what they did and the particular risk to the child," she said.

"They must also engage with therapeutic interventions which are tailored for the individualised risk that the person poses – not general programmes which are not specific to the individual. Then and only then should contact be considered to be supervised."

She added that the person doing the potential supervising must also undergo "protective assessments" that identify any education they may need to in order to properly hold the parent to account and ensure the child in question was protected.

Lucy said she had had no idea of her ex-husband's offending until police knocked on their door with a search warrant to seize his devices and arrested him.

She described feeling like an "indirect victim" of his crimes and has called for greater support for family members of sex offenders who experience their own kind of trauma.

"Whilst I can't imagine what the children in the [indecent] pictures have gone through, and there's a part of me that almost doesn't let my brain go there, what happened from the door knock completely broke our lives," she said.

"And the before is this lovely time of innocence, of believing somebody at face value, of believing that people are safe.

"Since the door knock, nobody is safe and I struggle with that.

"Our whole lives have being totally and utterly upended and still continue to be so, that whilst we're not direct victims, we're certainly indirect victims."

She said she and her child had to leave the family home and relocate to another area – to protect the child from the "horror of the truth" about their father.

Despite initial contact with social services, in which Lucy said she had to be deemed fit to parent her own child, there was no further support – particularly around the time of her ex-husband's court case.

"Why isn't there a system in place to tell family members ahead of that to prepare us or to make sure that we're safe?" she said.

"You're totally on your own. There are no organisations in Northern Ireland, there's no local support to help family members deal with this, so where do I go to next to get the help for what happens next?"

Geraldine Hanna said crimes of the type Lucy's husband was convicted of were "devastating" and "land like a bomb" in people's lives.

"This case really highlights the broader ripple impact of crime," she said.

"We don't often think about the wider impact... that it has on those who are associated with the accused in such crimes.

"So if that's your partner, your husband, the father of your children, there is real need to ensure that there's clear pathways to support for you in that case, so that you have the information and that independent support and information to help you make informed decisions and that you're supported through the journey as well."

Lucy said much of her life after her ex-husband's crimes were uncovered had been "a blur" and "horrific".

"Every now and then when something happens through court or something happens with the case, I go right back to the door knock - of the days after the door knock that were so horrific," she added.

"And I don't think we will ever be able to move fully on from that."

articles.title: Swept away by Ganga 15 days ago, Bihar woman found in UP
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: For 15 days, Sunaina Devi (55) survived on river water and the fragile shelter of a half-submerged thatched hut, after being swept 50km dow.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For 15 days, Sunaina Devi (55) survived on river water and the fragile shelter of a half-submerged thatched hut, after being swept 50km downstream by the monsoon-swollen Ganga. She was found alive Monday by fishermen who heard her cries.Devi, from Kapurpatti village in Bihar's Buxar district, had gone to bathe on Aug 30 when the current pulled her under. Her son, Govinda Gond, filed a missing person report at Itarhi police station. Her family did not know she had drifted across the state border into Chain Chhapra village in UP's Ballia, on the other side of the river, soon after falling in.In Chain Chhapra, Devi managed to grab an abandoned hut in a field and pull herself up. Surrounded by floodwater, she survived by drinking from the same Ganga that had nearly drowned her.On Monday she collapsed and slipped once again into floodwater. Mallah fishermen in boats heard her chants of "Shivguru-Sh-ivguru", spotted her behind sarpat grass and pulled her aboard.Hunger strike studies in British Medical Journal say with water intake, the body can survive without food for 21 to 40 days."It was miraculous," Haldi SHO Rajiv Kumar Rai told TOI. Police gave her food and water and determined her identity.The family had feared the worst. "There was no update for so many days we genuinely thought we'd lost her," Govinda said.Police said relatives broke down in tears when they saw her. "They were not expecting to find her alive. The reunion was emotional and raw," Rai said.Her husband, Janardhan, a farmer, told TOI, "Deep down, there was still a flickering hope."Devi is still dazed. "It feels like my mind stops at one place. It was very difficult to be alone for so many days. I didn't know I had such strength in me," she says.Her family says she remains weak. Doctors expect the disorientation to ease in a few days.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: RUPPs: Inside India's little-known political parties that recieve millions of dollars
articles.summary: Little-known political parties are receiving millions in donations despite limited electoral activity.
articles.body:
There was little to suggest that the locked flat in Anand, in the western Indian state of Gujarat, was the headquarters of a political party.

There was no signboard, campaign poster or obvious trace of political activity. But on paper, the Satyawadi Rakshak Party had recently received an extraordinary amount of money.

In the financial year ending in March 2024, official records show the Gujarat-based party received more than 3.3bn rupees (approx $35m; £25m) in donations. A few months later, when India held the world's largest general election, it fielded a single candidate, who lost his deposit.

Its accounts say that 84.8m rupees went towards election campaigning, while more than 3.16bn rupees were listed as spending on "public welfare".

"We have spent the money on charity but have not maintained records," said Swati Ben Patel, the party's president, who lives in the same residential complex as its registered office.

The party is one of more than 2,800 Registered Unrecognised Political Parties, or RUPPs - a vast but little-known tier of Indian politics. These parties are legally registered but have not won enough votes or seats to be recognised at the state or national level.

Some contest elections only sporadically or field a handful of candidates. Yet, like larger parties, they can receive donations and claim tax exemptions. Donors can also reduce their taxable income through eligible contributions.

The rules are intended to support political activity, but tax officials say they can be misused.

A months-long BBC investigation examined six RUPPs that reported some of the largest donations in 2023-24. Together, they received about 17bn rupees, despite fielding just 15 candidates in the 2024 election. None came close to winning.

The gap between the money some parties receive and their limited electoral presence has drawn increasing scrutiny from India's tax authorities.

An internal Income Tax department document reviewed by the BBC shows that officials have been investigating suspected misuse of RUPPs since at least 2022.

It identifies 55.91bn rupees in suspected bogus political donations made by taxpayers seeking tax benefits, as well as 6.65bn rupees in foreign transactions. It also notes possible violations of tax, foreign-funding and election laws.

None of the six parties examined by the BBC has been publicly named in these wider inquiries. The BBC has not established that any of them committed financial wrongdoing.

But in several cases, it found a striking gap between the way the organisations were described in their records and what reporters encountered on the ground.

Some registered offices were closed or appeared inactive. Party officials sometimes said they did not control their organisations' finances or could not explain how large sums had been spent.

The BBC found signs that the political presence of some of these parties was limited. Although their websites sometimes carried photographs of door-to-door canvassing, one candidate, Indradevi Hiralal of the Garib Kalyan Party, said she had not visited her constituency to campaign in 2024. She showed a single poster printed for the election.

There were also signs of scrutiny from the authorities. Three parties said they or their officials had faced action by the Income Tax department. At a fourth, a relative of a party official said the family home had been searched. The other two denied facing such action.

Tax authorities in Bihar, Gujarat and Delhi, as well as the Central Board of Direct Taxes, did not respond to questions about whether any of the six parties had been investigated or subjected to searches.

Of the six parties, Aam Janmat Party reported receiving the most money.

Founded in Patna in 2020, it reported no individual donations above 20,000 rupees - the threshold at which donors must be identified to the Election Commission - during its first two years.

Aam Janmat Party reported 2.16bn rupees in donations in 2022-23. The following year, the figure nearly tripled to more than 6.2bn rupees - more than twice the roughly 2.8bn rupees received by the Indian National Congress, the country's main opposition party.

Aam Janmat Party officials could not explain the sudden rise.

Aam Janmat Party party fielded just one candidate in the 2024 general election. He received a tiny share of the vote and lost his deposit.

The BBC traced its founding president, Anamika Paswan, to Patna city in Bihar state. Paswan, now a vice-president of the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the state, said she had resigned from Aam Janmat in 2022.

When reporters later sought documents relating to her departure, Paswan was not present. Her husband produced what he said was her resignation letter and another document stating that the party had moved hundreds of miles west to Ahmedabad in Gujarat state with Gaurav Mishra as its president.

But the office at its registered address there was shut.

Its treasurer, Dharmendra Vaishnav, said by telephone that Aam Janmat had "shut operations". He said he knew nothing about its finances and directed questions to Mishra, who did not respond to repeated calls and messages.

The party's listed bank account, however, could still receive money. The BBC transferred a small donation and the payment went through.

The registered office of the Garib Kalyan Party was also closed.

It reported receiving 1.38bn rupees in donations in 2023-24, but fielded just three candidates in the general election.

At the home of its president Neeraj Kumar Kshatriya, his mother said she knew little about the party. But she recalled Income Tax department officials searching the family home, although she did not know why.

Researchers who track political finance say the pattern raises questions about what these parties do with the money they receive.

"These parties are not electorally active, yet they are getting such huge funds and they are spending the money as well," said Shelly Mahajan, a researcher at the Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog.

But tracing such transactions can be difficult. Tax officials told the BBC that money can pass through a web of taxpayers, political parties and intermediaries, obscuring where it came from and where it ultimately went.

The BBC could not establish that any donations to the six parties had been returned in this way.

It did, however, trace two people listed as donors to the New India United Party who said they had claimed tax benefits on their contributions.

One Ahmedabad resident confirmed donating 500,000 rupees. The other said he had donated on a friend's advice. "I did it as a way to save tax, and have declared the same," he said, adding that the authorities had not contacted him.

Three tax officials in Ahmedabad, Delhi and Patna, speaking on condition of anonymity, said chartered accountants and other middlemen can connect taxpayers seeking deductions with parties willing to receive donations.

In some cases, they said, intermediaries can also exercise considerable control over party finances.

Surender Tiwari said that was what happened at his Swatantrata Abhivyakti Party, which reported receiving 2.19bn rupees in donations in 2023-24.

Although he was its president, Tiwari said he did not control the party's money. Its chartered accountant handled the finances and gave him campaign funds, he said.

"The chartered accountant gave me some money for the election campaign," Tiwari said. "He would then show videos of the campaign to clients who wanted to get tax relief through donations."

Tiwari said the party received a notice from the Income Tax department in July and accused its chartered accountant Mayur Singh of keeping him "in the dark".

Singh denied wrongdoing. He said his role was limited to preparing audit reports that parties must submit to the Election Commission, although he acknowledged working for several examined by the BBC.

"Try to understand, it's the same people behind these parties," he said, without elaborating.

Concerns surrounding India's little-known parties extend beyond their finances. The Election Commission has also been trying to remove inactive parties from its official list.

Last year, it delisted more than 800 RUPPs that had not fielded a candidate in six years. But it cannot cancel a party's legal registration, limiting the effect of such action.

The BBC asked the commission whether tax authorities had shared information about suspected financial irregularities involving RUPPs, including the six examined. It did not respond.

As scrutiny grows, the challenge for authorities will be to establish who controls these parties, where their money comes from and how it is ultimately spent.

articles.title: Worried about taking a sick day? What that says about you
articles.summary: As many as half of people report working when sick. The reasons for this are complex, experts say.
articles.body:
You wake up feeling unwell but there's a big day at work ahead.

What do you do? If the answer is to go in (or log on), you're not alone.

Research suggests anywhere between a third to a half of people in the UK work even when sick - something experts call presenteeism.

And your approach to sickness says a lot about you as an individual and where you work.

"The younger generation get the snowflake tag thrown at them, but it's not true," says University of Manchester psychologist Prof Sir Cary Cooper, who is one of the world's leading experts on workplace wellbeing.

Workers aged 16 to 24 took an average of 2.4 days off sick last year, compared to 6.2 days for those aged 50 to 64.

Sir Cary, who has advised the UK government on employment policies in this area, says there are several reasons for this.

Younger workers are more likely to work in roles where there is little security, such as zero-hours contracts.

They are also less likely to suffer from long-term health conditions and joint problems that are major contributors to sickness absence.

But Sir Cary adds: "I think younger generations do have higher expectations about how employers should treat them and consider their wellbeing.

"Older generations have perhaps been more willing to put up with things, but that doesn't necessarily make that approach healthy.

"When it comes to taking time off, younger workers seem more willing to view mental wellbeing as part of their overall health rather than something that should simply be pushed through."

There are a variety of factors that influence someone's approach to sickness absence.

For some, work is closely tied to identity. Occupational psychologists call this work centrality - and research links this to greater engagement, commitment and willingness to go the extra mile.

If work is central to who you are, being absent can feel like temporarily losing part of yourself.

"These people feel a strong desire to keep showing up," says Dr Audrey Tang, a psychologist who writes about workplace wellbeing.

She says those working in caring professions such as medicine, nursing and teaching have a particular tendency towards this.

"They often report they would rather have a physical accident to have a reason not to show up than just take the day off."

Others fear being seen as weak or lazy. Younger workers are particularly susceptible to this, says Tang.

"They're more likely to be early in their profession and they don't want to leave a negative impression."

Workplace culture and behaviour can have a significant influence on people's willingness to take time off sick, says psychologist Dr Tara Quinn-Cirillo.

When teams are stretched and there is little or no cover, employees know their absence will increase the workload for colleagues.

"The role of guilt and shame is significant in a toxic organisation that prioritises productivity over health and wellbeing," says Quinn-Cirillo.

"There is a 'carry-on' culture in some workplaces that encourages people to keep going when they should be resting."

Such cultures reward presenteeism. Employees feel valued for turning up regardless of how they are feeling and staff quickly absorb the message if managers praise people for working through illness.

"In a healthy work environment, people should be able to have open and honest conversations about wellbeing and sick days," says Quinn-Cirillo.

Trust also matters. If absence is routinely questioned or viewed negatively, workers can become reluctant to take legitimate time off for fear of being judged.

That, says Quinn-Cirillo, is a "huge red flag".

How to know when you're too sick to work

Deciding whether you are too sick to work is not always straightforward.

For physical illness, Tang says there are some well-established rules of thumb.

"If you're vomiting and have diarrhoea or have a fever, you should stay at home for 48 hours and 24 hours respectively after the symptoms have passed. In those situations, you're unlikely to be able to work effectively anyway."

Beyond that, the decision becomes more nuanced, according to Tang.

"Where there is more of a grey area is with coughs and colds. Since Covid, workplace etiquette has changed - generally it's considered polite to work from home."

But she says an absolute must is that mental health should be treated no differently than physical health.

"If you're sick and unable to work, you're sick and unable to work."

Quinn-Cirillo adds: "Ultimately it's about capacity to do a job, whether it be physical or mental health."

A further warning sign is when work starts affecting basic self-care, she says.

"Is your ability to look after yourself changing? Are you able to decompress from work? Is your sleep OK?"

If the answer is no, it may be a sign that rest is exactly what is needed.

articles.title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
articles.summary: Supporters of the scheme say the bank would enable governments to get cheaper loans to spend on defence projects.
articles.body:
The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank, aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity."

Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister.

He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine.

He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions.

"Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine – but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine."

It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The DSRB is a multilateral bank aimed at providing cheaper loans to fund defence projects and has backing from Albania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

Membership of the bank for the UK and other G7 countries would come with an upfront investment cost of around £870m spread over three years.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

The government has so far avoided committing to raising defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, only repeating the longer term goal of 3.5% by 2035.

As defence secretary, Healey privately pushed for the UK to join the DSRB as a means of raising money.

He resigned in June, accusing the Treasury of being unwilling to provide the resources needed to defend the country.

In his resignation letter, he said there were "credible ways" to fund extra defence spending, including "working multinationally".

A government spokesperson said: "We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity.

"We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary."

articles.title: Candace Owens moves to dismiss Brian Harpole’s defamation lawsuit over explosive Charlie Kirk assassination claims
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Candace Owens is asking a federal judge to dismiss Brian Harpole’s defamation lawsuit, arguing that her comments about the former Charlie Kirk securit.
articles.body: Candace Owens is asking a federal judge to dismiss Brian Harpole’s defamation lawsuit, arguing that her comments about the former Charlie Kirk security chief were protected speech rather than actionable false statements. The motion puts the focus on free speech, public debate and the legal line between opinion and defamation as the case moves through federal court in Tennessee.Candace Owens challenges Brian Harpole defamation claimsHarpole filed the lawsuit in April against Owens, Candace Owens LLC, GeorgeTom Inc. and Mitchell Snow. The case, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, accuses the defendants of making statements that linked Harpole to an alleged plot surrounding Kirk’s assassination. The court docket confirms the case remains active.Owens now wants all six claims against her and her companies dismissed. Her attorneys argue that several statements cited by Harpole were opinions, rhetorical exaggeration or questions rather than factual allegations that could form the basis of a defamation claim.Among the comments at issue are Owens saying Harpole and members of Kirk’s security team “should be fired.” Her lawyers contend that such language represents a judgment about security performance rather than a factual statement capable of being proven true or false.The filing also challenges Harpole’s allegation that Owens portrayed him as someone who effectively allowed Kirk’s death to happen. Her legal team argues that the lawsuit attempts to turn a collection of individual statements into a broader defamatory meaning that Owens did not directly state.Harpole, meanwhile, disputes the allegations and has maintained that the claims surrounding him are false. His lawsuit says he was in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2025, rather than at Fort Huachuca in Arizona, where Snow allegedly claimed to have seen him. Harpole has also argued that travel records support his account.Fort Huachuca allegation remains central to lawsuitThe dispute over Fort Huachuca is one of the most significant factual issues hanging over the case. Harpole says he never attended the alleged meeting, while Snow has defended his account. Harpole’s later court filing argues that Snow’s description and confidence in the identification helped give the allegation an appearance of certainty.Owens’ current motion does not fully resolve that factual dispute. Instead, her attorneys say the issue can be addressed later if the lawsuit survives the dismissal stage.Another major argument concerns Harpole’s status in the public debate surrounding Kirk’s killing. Owens’ lawyers say Harpole voluntarily entered the controversy before Owens publicly identified him. They argue that this could make him a limited-purpose public figure, potentially requiring him to prove actual malice.Owens is also invoking Tennessee’s Public Participation Act, an anti-SLAPP law designed to protect certain speech concerning matters of public concern. Her lawyers argue that commentary about Kirk’s assassination and the security operation falls within that protection.If Owens succeeds under that law, she is asking the court to award attorneys’ fees and related costs.For now, however, none of the competing allegations has been resolved by the court. The lawsuit remains pending, and the judge has yet to rule on Owens’ request to dismiss the claims.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump administration approves sending powerful bombs to Israel in $2.8 billion weapons sale
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago. The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 of the bombs, made up of 20,000 Mk84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to two U.S. officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss the package, which is not yet final. Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing — in which U.S. taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States. The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israeli’s military capacity. The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The U.S. brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued. The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas. The sale signals that some strains in the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, especially since the two countries launched the war against Iran in February, are not impeding the closeness of the U.S.-Israeli alliance. Trump has had a hot-and-cold history with Netanyahu over the years and expressed some frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House. In 2024, the Biden administration held off on one shipment of the bombs, but Trump lifted that hold when he took office again. Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January. The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants, with some designed to penetrate deep, underground targets while others detonate above ground and cause widespread damage. Though the Israeli military has offered few details about what bombs and artillery it has used in Gaza, experts analyzing strike footage and blast fragments found on-site believe the U.S.-made bombs have been used there, targeting a tunnel network used by Hamas but also killing of people in densely populated areas. While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the fragile ceasefire took hold in October, Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the territory, including some overnight and into Tuesday that killed several people. That is even after Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a key Mideast negotiator, met with Netanyahu last month in an effort to push the ceasefire deal forward and asked Israel to reduce its attacks. Militants have carried out shooting attacks on Israeli troops, and Israel says its strikes are in response to those and other ceasefire violations. The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel in 2023 killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Israel’s offensive in Gaza to retaliate has killed more than 73,264 Palestinians, including those killed since the ceasefire, Gaza’s Health Ministry said.
